2. 
Agency Reversing Course. In both State Farm (discussed in Chapter 
5) and FCC v. Fox, the agencies reversed prior agency policy choices. Should 
that matter? And, if so, how?
Appellate and trial courts have struggled to answer these questions and 
apply the reasoning in State Farm and Fox. Courts applying Fox recognize it 
as granting agencies flexibihty to alter policies. Modesto Irrigation Dist. v. 
Gutierrez, 619 F.3d 1024 (9th Cir. 2010); Westar Energy, Inc. v. FERC, 568 F.3d 
985 (D.C. Cir. 2009). Courts have, however, required that the agency at least 
exphcitly acknowledge and explain a departure from prior policy. See Phillip 
Morris USA, Inc. v. Vilsack, 736 F.3d 284, 290 (4th Cir. 2013) fWe defer to the 
agency’s new position no less than the old, so long as we are satisfied that the 
agency’s change in position was intentional and considered.”); Modesto 
Irrigation, 619 F.3d at 1034; Dillmon v. Natl Transp. Safety Bd., 588 F.3d 
1085, 1091 (D.C. Cir. 2009) (holding that courts will not “assume [an agency] 
has engaged in reasoned decision making^’ if it ‘‘implicitly” departs from prior 
precedent without explanation). Accordingly, the D.C. Circuit has held that the 
“core requirement” an agency must meet when changing course is to “ ‘provide 
[a] reasoned explanation for its action,’ which ‘would ordinarily demand that it 
display awareness that it is changing position.’ ” Natl Ass’n of Home Builders 
V. EPA, 682 F.3d 1032, 1038 (D.C. Cir. 2012) (quoting Fox).
3. 
The Role of Political Explanations. Justice Scalia in a portion of his 
opinion not excerpted above noted, with apparent approval, that pohtical 
pressure from Congress appeared to have been a primary impetus for the 
FCC’s decision to change its pohcy regarding fleeting expletives. The 
dissenting justices found this fact troubling. Justice Breyer argued that the 
APA “does not permit [independent administrative agencies] to make pohcy 
choices for purely pohtical reasons.”
The relevance and appropriateness of pohtical reasons depends upon what 
we mean by “pohtical.” Sierra Club v. Costle, discussed in Chapter 5, makes 
clear that contacts and discussions with pohtical overseers will not invalidate 
a rulemaking proceeding where the rule is appropriately justified by reference 
to the considerations made relevant in the agency’s statute. But pohtical 
pressure that causes an administrator to take into account considerations that 
are properly excluded by the agency’s mandate might be invahdating.
On the other hand, where pohtical values or ideological commitment is 
what we mean by pohtics, there presumably are contexts in which such 
considerations would be appropriate. So long as these preferences do not 
contradict exphcit statutory mandates, agency judgments about priorities are 
likely to be free from judicial review. For a discussion of the use of pohtical 
reason in administration, see JERRY L. Ma SHAW, REASONED ADMINISTRATION:
